Early colonial and state law codes included blasphemy prohibitions drawn from English common law and biblical norms. These provisions reflected a pragmatic recognition that open derision of the religion that shaped social norms, family structure, and legal concepts of individual dignity undermines public order. Unrestrained mockery carries tangible social costs. When Christian doctrines are recast as objects of crude satire or institutional contempt, the ethical vocabulary available to the broader culture contracts. Concepts such as forgiveness, sacrificial love, and objective moral truth lose public force. Over decades this has coincided with measurable declines in family formation, rising rates of substance abuse and social isolation, and reduced deference to authority institutions. Blasphemy functions as a solvent rather than neutral expression. It signals that nothing is off-limits and that the majority faith, unlike protected secular identities, may be attacked without cost. Clear statutory boundaries would deter the most inflammatory public acts while leaving room for serious theological or historical debate.

Free speech under the First Amendment was never understood as an unlimited right to wound the foundational beliefs of the polity. Historical practice permitted restrictions on blasphemy alongside limits on obscenity and defamation. Contemporary constitutional doctrine already recognizes narrow categories of unprotected speech. A carefully drafted blasphemy statute would sit among them: conduct that deliberately subjects the Trinity, the divinity of Christ, the resurrection, or the Virgin Mary to public ridicule or severe disparagement. This is distinguishable from protected academic inquiry or internal religious criticism. The state has a legitimate interest in preserving the religious conventions that once animated its highest achievements. Provisions could include safe harbors for private conversation, genuine scholarly analysis, and any expression lacking the element of public insult.

Objections that such laws violate neutrality or the Establishment Clause overlook the cultural reality: Christianity is not one interchangeable creed among many but the historical majority faith that provided the symbolic and ethical architecture within which the Constitution itself was written and interpreted for generations. A targeted statute acknowledges this inheritance without requiring universal religious observance or suppressing minority practices. "Blasphemy" would be defined as any public act, statement, image, or performance that, by clear intent, insults, ridicules, or subjects to severe contempt a core Christian doctrine, personage of divine significance, or recognized Christian institution when the conduct would reasonably inflame offense among believers. Penalties scale with repetition and audience size. Courts would enforce with the same restraint they apply to other speech limitations, focusing on objective elements of public dissemination and intent rather than vague hurt feelings. Private citizens retain full liberty to reject faith; the prohibition targets only the public weaponization of contempt.

These laws would serve several concrete ends. They would discourage the ritualized humiliation of Christian symbols in art and entertainment, which currently functions as a low-cost signal of elite sophistication. They would reduce the incentive for activist groups to use blasphemy-style provocation to manufacture outrage cycles. They would restore to believers the same baseline dignity Western societies now extend to other protected characteristics. Most importantly, they would slow the substitution of adversarial secularism for the inherited moral language of the founding era.

The alternative—continued legal tolerance of ritualistic scorn toward the religion that formed its laws and customs—has already produced widespread cynicism and weakened institutions. Enacting narrow, enforceable blasphemy provisions directed at insults against Christian beliefs, figures, and institutions is a practical step toward resecuring the cultural preconditions of stable self-government. In Defense of Reverence: The Case for an American Blasphemy Law

No society has ever permitted everything to be said about everything. Every legal order on earth draws lines through speech — around libel, around threats, around incitement, around obscenity, around the secrets of the state and the dignity of the courtroom. The honest question is never whether speech will be bounded. It is which harms a people take seriously enough to forbid. A nation that criminalizes a false accusation but shrugs at the public degradation of the faith of most of its citizens has made a choice about what matters. It has decided that reputation is sacred and God is not. This essay argues that America should choose differently: that federal and state law should once again make it a crime to publicly, maliciously, and scurrilously vilify the Christian religion, its central figures, and its institutions — and that if the First Amendment as currently construed forbids this, the Constitution should be amended.

I. The American Tradition

What I propose is not an alien import. It is a restoration. For the first century and a half of the Republic, blasphemy was a crime, and no one thought this contradicted American liberty. In People v. Ruggles (1811), Chancellor James Kent — the father of American jurisprudence — upheld the conviction of a man who had publicly reviled Christ in the vilest terms. Kent's reasoning was precise: the law did not punish error of opinion, which remained free, but "maliciously reviling" that which the people hold sacred, speech whose tendency is "to corrupt the morals of the people, and to destroy good order." Pennsylvania reached the same conclusion in Updegraph v. Commonwealth (1824), holding Christianity woven into the common law itself. Abner Kneeland, the last American jailed for blasphemy, served his sentence in Massachusetts in 1838 — nearly half a century after the First Amendment was ratified, and no court saw a conflict. Prosecutions and convictions persisted into the twentieth century.

The rupture came late and came suddenly: Joseph Burstyn, Inc. v. Wilson in 1952, striking down a ban on "sacrilegious" films, built atop the newly-incorporated Establishment Clause of Everson (1947). A settlement that had endured for 150 years was dismantled in a generation. And even at the height of that dismantling, the Court in Beauharnais v. Illinois (1952) upheld group libel — the principle that the law may protect a people's collective dignity from defamation. The premise of this essay has never been alien to American law. It was the American law.

II. Speech Is Already Bounded — The Only Question Is Whose Injuries Count

The absolutist objection collapses on contact with reality. Defamation, fraud, perjury, true threats, incitement, obscenity, fighting words: all are speech, all are crimes. In Chaplinsky v. New Hampshire (1942), the Court held unprotected those words "which by their very utterance inflict injury." Consider, then, what public blasphemy is by its very utterance: a deliberate injury inflicted on the deepest identity of believing men and women — the grandmother who hears her Savior spat upon in the public square, the child taught that reverence is ridiculous. We accept that a racial slur hurled in a stranger's face may be punished because of the wound it inflicts on contact. The devout believer's wound is not lesser. To protect every human dignity except the religious one is not principle; it is a hierarchy of sympathies dressed up as one.

III. The Democratic World Does It

The proposal is said to be theocratic. Then Germany is a theocracy: §166 of its criminal code punishes insults to religious communities in a manner suited to disturb the public peace, and it remains in force. Poland's Article 196, protecting religious feelings, is still invoked in prosecutions. Austria, Italy, and Finland maintain analogous laws. Ireland, Canada, Denmark, and New Zealand repealed their blasphemy statutes only within the last decade — meaning that for their entire modern histories, these were liberal democracies with free presses, raucous atheists, and blasphemy laws, all at once. The European Court of Human Rights has repeatedly held that protecting religious feelings is a legitimate aim compatible with freedom of expression, upholding convictions in Otto-Preminger-Institut v. Austria (1994) and E.S. v. Austria (2018). The bogeyman invoked against this proposal is Pakistan, with its executions. The model on offer is Munich: narrow statutes, modest fines, no inquisitions — and Christopher Hitchens and Richard Dawkins on the bestseller lists the whole time. The European experience refutes the claim that reverence and robust debate cannot coexist. They coexist wherever the law targets degradation rather than doubt.

IV. Why Christianity

Why protect one faith? For the same reason we nearly amended the Constitution to protect one flag. The flag-desecration amendment passed the House repeatedly and failed the Senate by a single vote in 2006 — proof that Americans understand, in their bones, that a people may forbid the desecration of its constitutive symbol. Christianity is America's constitutive symbol in a far deeper register. Tocqueville observed that religion was "the first of America's political institutions"; our calendar, our oaths, our motto, our moral grammar, our very conception of the person are downstream of the Christian inheritance, and roughly six in ten Americans still claim the faith as their own. Law routinely protects specifically enumerated interests; specificity is not discrimination. Nor does protecting Christian doctrine punish anyone else's conscience: the Jew, the Muslim, the atheist lose no right to disbelieve, to argue, to publish, to persuade. They lose only a license to degrade. And nothing in the statute's logic forbids extending its protection to other faiths in time — but a law may rationally begin where the wound and the heritage are.

V. The Constitutional Path

Candor requires admitting what current doctrine forbids. Under Everson and Burstyn, a Christian blasphemy statute would likely be struck down today. The answer is not despair but Article V. The Constitution has been amended to correct the errors of courts before; an amendment protecting the sacred from public desecration would do precisely what the flag amendment nearly did, for an object immeasurably worthier. The founding generation — which prosecuted blasphemers while celebrating freedom of conscience — would be astonished to learn that the Amendment they wrote now protects what they punished. If a half-century of living constitutionalism moved the document's meaning, a democratic amendment may move it back. That is not an assault on the Constitution. It is the Constitution working as designed.

VI. A Narrow Statute

The parade of horribles dissolves on inspection of a properly drafted law. Criminalize only public vilification: speech intended to degrade, uttered in scurrilous or grossly offensive terms, in a manner tending to disturb the public peace. Exempt scholarship, journalism, serious art, doctrinal debate among the churches, and all good-faith criticism however severe. Grade the penalties — fines first, misdemeanors for the obdurate — to deter without martyring. "Who decides what offends?" Juries do, under instruction, exactly as they decide what is obscene, what is threatening, what is libel today; the law does not abandon those judgments because they are hard. "Slippery slope?" Slopes are managed by elements and exemptions, not by abstinence. Reasoned atheism remains perfectly legal. Sober denial of the faith was lawful even under Chancellor Kent. The statute's target is narrower and worthier: the deliberate public degradation of what a people holds holy.

VII. The Deeper Stake

The gentlest objection comes from within the faith itself: did Christ not command his followers to turn the other cheek? He did — to his followers, bearing their own crosses. He gave no such instruction to the magistrate, who, as Paul wrote, "beareth not the sword in vain." Kent saw this clearly two centuries ago: the blasphemy law guards not the honor of God, who needs no defense, but the peace and morals of the people, who do — the faith of the vulnerable, the reverence of the young, the shared sacred canopy under which a diverse society must somehow live as neighbors. A republic that will not defend that canopy will eventually defend nothing, because it will have taught itself that nothing is worth defending. Law is a teacher. For two generations it has taught that the holy is fair game and scorn is a right. It is time it taught something older and truer: that liberty without reverence decays into license, and that a people wise enough to fence its sacred things is a people that still knows how to be free.

While the emotional appeal of protecting Christianity from insult is understandable, blasphemy laws would: ✅ Violate the First Amendment (free speech & establishment clauses). ✅ Create a slippery slope toward censorship (who decides what’s "blasphemous"?). ✅ Discriminate against non-Christian religions. ✅ Stifle art, satire, and scientific debate. ✅ Undermine America’s reputation as a free speech leader. ✅ Backfire by making Christianity appear weak or intolerant.

This argument holds that certain expressions, while protected by free speech, may cross the line into "public decency" or "obscenity" when attacking religion.

  • Setting Boundaries: Blasphemy laws could draw a clearer line between legitimate criticism and malicious insult, preventing the latter from becoming public discourse.
  • Protecting Institutions: Beyond beliefs themselves, religious figures (such as Jesus or the Virgin Mary) and institutions (such as the Church) are seen by believers as sacred. Protecting them could be viewed as respecting the historical and cultural heritage of society.

3. Preventing "Hate Speech"

While U.S. hate speech laws focus on protected characteristics like race, gender, and sexual orientation, some extend this logic to religion:

  • Linking Religion to Identity: For many, religion is a core part of personal identity. Attacking their faith could be perceived as a personal attack.

Despite the above theoretical "benefits," implementing such laws in the U.S. would face significant constitutional and practical hurdles:

  • First Amendment Barrier: The Supreme Court has repeatedly affirmed that the government cannot regulate expression based on its content, especially religious content. Such a law would almost certainly be challenged as unconstitutional.

  • Chilling Effect: Even if not actively enforced, such laws could stifle public discourse, causing people to self-censor out of fear of legal consequences, thus damaging the marketplace of ideas.

Conclusion

While some might argue that blasphemy laws protecting Christian beliefs could safeguard social stability, uphold public morality, and align with global norms, these theoretical benefits are vastly outweighed by the constitutional principles and pluralistic values that define the United States. The First Amendment's protection of free speech, including the right to criticize or even satirize religion, is a cornerstone of American democracy. In practice, the U.S. addresses harmful speech through social norms, counter-speech, and existing laws against harassment, defamation, and true threats, rather than through broad blasphemy statutes.
